response.question: Someone is selling products with my registered trademark on them. What can I do?
response.answer:
Selling products with your registered trade mark may be infringement, but it depends on the facts. For example, use in trade by someone who is not the owner or a permitted user can infringe where the mark and goods meet the conditions in the law. Offering goods for sale under the mark counts as use. [trade_marks_act_1999:29]

A valid registration gives its owner the right to obtain relief for infringement, subject to conditions and limitations. The sources provided do not explain the available remedies or how to pursue them. [trade_marks_act_1999:28]

A sale is not automatically infringement just because it involves your mark. For example, the law provides protection in certain circumstances for resale of lawfully acquired goods put on the market by you or with your consent. That protection does not apply if you have legitimate reasons to oppose further dealings, such as a change or impairment in the goods’ condition. [trade_marks_act_1999:30]

response.question: Can I sue someone for using my brand name if I never registered it?
response.answer:
Yes, you may be able to sue even if you never registered your brand name. The law recognises a claim called “passing off” for an unregistered trade mark used in business. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

A passing-off suit can concern another person’s use of a mark that is identical to yours or so similar that it is likely to deceive or cause confusion. Whether you have a viable claim depends on the facts. The suit must be filed in a District Court with jurisdiction, not a lower court. [trade_marks_act_1999:134] [trade_marks_act_1999:2]

In a passing-off suit, a court may grant an injunction—an order to stop the conduct—and, at your option, damages or an account of profits. Monetary relief is subject to limitations. [trade_marks_act_1999:135]

response.question: Why could my trademark application be rejected?
response.answer:
Your application could be refused for several reasons. Which ones matter depends on your mark and the goods or services in your application.

• The mark does not distinguish your goods or services from others, or consists only of descriptive or commonly used trade terms. But prior use may have made it distinctive, or it may be a well-known mark. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
• It could deceive or confuse the public; hurt religious sentiments; contain scandalous or obscene material; or use a prohibited emblem or name. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
• It consists only of a product shape that results from the nature of the goods, is necessary for a technical result, or gives the goods substantial value. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
• It is identical or similar to an earlier mark for identical or similar goods or services, and the public is likely to be confused, including by thinking the marks are connected. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]
• It is identical or similar to an earlier mark that is well known in India, even for different goods or services, if using it without good reason would unfairly benefit from or harm the earlier mark’s distinctiveness or reputation. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]
• Its use could be stopped under copyright law or the law protecting an unregistered mark used in trade, known as passing off. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

For the last two grounds, the earlier mark’s owner must raise the objection in opposition proceedings—a formal challenge to registration. Consent from the owner of an earlier mark or right may also be relevant. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

The Registrar may accept an application with changes or conditions rather than refuse it. If the Registrar refuses it or accepts it conditionally, the reasons and materials used must be recorded in writing. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]

response.question: How long is a trademark registration valid and how do I renew it?
response.answer:
An Indian trade mark registration made after the Act commenced lasts 10 years. It can be renewed for further 10-year periods. Each renewal runs from the expiry of the previous registration period. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

To renew, the registered owner must apply in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed period, and pay the prescribed fee. The sources provided do not specify the form, fee amount or ordinary application deadline. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

If the registration has expired, the Registrar must renew it if the required application, fee and surcharge are submitted within six months of expiry. If the mark is removed for non-payment, an application for restoration may be made after six months and within one year of expiry; restoration is subject to the Registrar being satisfied that it is just. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

International registrations have separate provisions: they last 10 years and can be renewed for 10 years. A six-month grace period is available, subject to a surcharge. [trade_marks_act_1999:36G]

response.question: Can I use a song in my YouTube video without permission?
response.answer:
Sometimes, but not automatically. Using a copyrighted song in a YouTube video without permission can infringe copyright unless an exception applies. Copyright includes exclusive rights over making a film using a musical work and communicating a sound recording to the public. [copyright_act_1957:14; copyright_act_1957:51]

One possible exception is fair dealing for criticism or review, or for reporting current events. Whether your use is fair dealing depends on the circumstances. For criticism or review, the law also requires an acknowledgement identifying the work and, subject to exceptions, its author. [copyright_act_1957:52]

Different rights may exist in the song and its recording, so permission for one does not necessarily cover everything. Performer’s rights may also matter. [copyright_act_1957:13; copyright_act_1957:38A]

response.question: How long does copyright last for a book after the author dies?
response.answer:
For a book published during the author’s lifetime, copyright generally lasts for 60 years starting on 1 January of the year after the author dies. For example, if the author died in 2020, the period runs from 1 January 2021 to 31 December 2080. [copyright_act_1957:22]

For a jointly authored book, the period is generally counted from the year after the last author dies. [copyright_act_1957:22]

Different rules can apply. For example, if the book and any adaptation were not published before the author’s death, the period may instead be counted from publication. A public performance or sale of sound recordings can also count as publication for this rule. [copyright_act_1957:24] Books published anonymously or under a pen name can also have a different term. response.question: My employer says they own the articles I wrote at work. Who owns the copyright?
response.answer:
It depends on your employment, the purpose of the articles and any agreement you have. The available information is not enough to decide who owns them.

response.question: Someone copied my book and is selling it. What legal action can I take?
response.answer:
If you own the relevant copyright and the copies are infringing, you may be able to take civil action. Selling infringing copies can be copyright infringement [copyright_act_1957:51]. Whether the copies are infringing depends on the facts, including any licence or applicable exception [copyright_act_1957:51; copyright_act_1957:52].

You may ask a court for an injunction, meaning an order to stop the infringement, and seek damages or an account of profits [copyright_act_1957:55]. You may also take proceedings to recover possession of infringing copies and equipment used or intended to produce them [copyright_act_1957:58].

If the defendant proves they did not know and had no reasonable grounds to believe copyright existed in the work, the available remedies are limited: an injunction and potentially some or all of their profits from selling the infringing copies [copyright_act_1957:55].

response.question: What is the jail punishment for copyright piracy?
response.answer:
For knowingly infringing copyright or helping someone else do so, the usual punishment is **six months to three years in jail**, plus a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. [copyright_act_1957:63]

response.question: Can someone challenge or oppose my patent?
response.answer:
Yes. Someone can oppose a patent application or challenge a granted patent, depending on the circumstances.

• Before grant: Once your application is published, any person can submit a written opposition to the Controller, the patent authority, before the patent is granted. [patents_act_1970:25]

• After grant: A “person interested” can give notice of opposition to the Controller after grant but before one year expires from the date the grant was published. This includes someone engaged in or promoting research in the same field. [patents_act_1970:25] [patents_act_1970:2]

Possible grounds include that the claimed invention was published before the relevant priority date, that it is obvious and lacks an inventive step, or that the patent description does not sufficiently and clearly explain the invention or how to perform it. The priority date is the relevant date for assessing a claim. [patents_act_1970:25]

In a post-grant opposition, the Controller considers recommendations from an Opposition Board and gives both sides an opportunity to be heard. The Controller can then maintain, amend or revoke the patent. [patents_act_1970:25]

A granted patent can also be challenged through a petition for revocation, meaning cancellation, or a counterclaim in an infringement suit, on specified grounds. [patents_act_1970:64]

response.question: What exclusive rights does copyright give me over my novel?
response.answer:
If you own the copyright in your novel, you have the exclusive right to do the following, or to give others permission to do them, in relation to the whole novel or any substantial part of it. These rights are subject to the provisions of the Act. [copyright_act_1957:14]

• Make copies, including storing the novel electronically. [copyright_act_1957:14]
• Issue copies to the public, other than copies already in circulation. A copy sold once counts as already in circulation. [copyright_act_1957:14]
• Perform the novel in public or communicate it to the public. [copyright_act_1957:14]
• Make a film or sound recording based on it. [copyright_act_1957:14]
• Make a translation or adaptation, such as a version in another form. [copyright_act_1957:14]
• Exercise the listed rights in relation to a translation or adaptation too. [copyright_act_1957:14]

The rights you personally hold may depend on whether you have assigned any of them to someone else. An assignment is a transfer of copyright rights. [copyright_act_1957:18]

Separately, as the author, you have the right to claim authorship. You may also restrain or claim damages for changes to the work that harm your honour or reputation, even if you have assigned the copyright. [copyright_act_1957:57]

response.question: Can my trademark be cancelled if I stop using it?
response.answer:
Yes. A registered trademark can be removed for non-use, but removal is not automatic. An affected person must apply to the Registrar or the High Court. Removal can concern particular goods or services covered by the registration. [trade_marks_act_1999:47]

One ground is that there has been no genuine use of the mark for those goods or services for a continuous period of at least five years, counted from when the mark was actually entered in the register. response.question: Is it a crime to sell fake branded goods?
response.answer:
Yes. Selling goods with a false trade mark or false trade description can be a crime. Even offering them for sale or keeping them for sale can be covered [trade_marks_act_1999:104].

A false trade mark can include a brand mark, or a confusingly similar mark, applied without the brand owner’s consent [trade_marks_act_1999:102].

The seller may avoid punishment by proving one of the following: they took all reasonable precautions and had no reason to suspect a problem; they gave the prosecutor all the information they had about their supplier when asked; or they otherwise acted innocently [trade_marks_act_1999:104].

The punishment is generally six months to three years in prison and a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. A court may impose a lower prison term or fine for adequate and special reasons recorded in its judgment [trade_marks_act_1999:104].

response.question: How do I apply to register my logo as a trademark?
response.answer:
To apply to register your logo as a trade mark:

1. If you claim to own the mark and use it or propose to use it, apply in writing to the Registrar in the prescribed manner. You do not have to be using it already. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]
2. Identify the goods or services for which you want registration. One application can cover different classes of goods or services, but a fee is payable for each class. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]
3. File at the Trade Marks Registry office for the area where your principal place of business in India is located. If you do not carry on business in India, the office is determined by the Indian address for service given in your application. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]
4. The Registrar may refuse the application, accept it, or accept it with changes or conditions. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]

response.question: What rights do I get once my patent is granted?
response.answer:
A granted patent gives you rights to stop certain activities in India without your consent. The rights depend on what your patent covers:

• Product patent: You can prevent others from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the product for those purposes in India. [patents_act_1970:48]
• Process patent: You can prevent others from using the process in India. You can also prevent them from using, offering for sale, selling or importing for those purposes a product obtained directly by that process. [patents_act_1970:48]

These rights have limits. For example, the patented invention may be used for experiments, research or teaching pupils. Certain government uses are also permitted. [patents_act_1970:47] In specified circumstances, such as a national emergency, a licence allowing someone else to work the invention may be granted. [patents_act_1970:92]

If you own the patent jointly, an agreement may change your co-ownership rights. Subject to the rules and any agreement, a co-owner generally needs the other owners’ consent to grant a licence or transfer their share. [patents_act_1970:50]

You may bring an infringement case, but monetary compensation is not automatic. For example, it cannot be awarded against someone who proves they did not know and had no reasonable grounds to believe the patent existed when the infringement occurred. [patents_act_1970:111]

response.answer:

response.question: A company copied my patented invention. What can a court order against them?
response.answer:
In a patent infringement lawsuit, a court may grant an injunction—an order requiring the company to stop the infringing activity. The court may also award damages, meaning money for loss, or an account of profits, meaning a remedy based on profits made from the infringement. These remedies are not automatic. [patents_act_1970:111; patents_act_1970:109]

There are important limits on monetary remedies:
• The court cannot award damages or an account of profits if the company proves that, when the infringement occurred, it did not know and had no reasonable grounds to believe the patent existed. This does not remove the court’s power to grant an injunction. [patents_act_1970:111]
• The court may refuse those monetary remedies for infringement during a period between a missed renewal fee deadline and an extension of that period. [patents_act_1970:111]
• If the patent specification was amended after publication, monetary remedies for use before the amendment was allowed are restricted, unless the court is satisfied that the original specification was prepared in good faith and with reasonable skill and knowledge. [patents_act_1970:111]
